title: Volim burek
reviewerNotes: Full draft to Lesson 1 exemplar bar. ready for human review before publish.
storyBeat: Ana’s food disasters begin with burek. Emir teaches likes and a gentle accusative chunk.

vocabulary: Food words: burek, sirnica, zeljanica, hljeb, jogurt
Hungry: gladan / gladna; ukusno; dobar tek
culture: In BiH, burek means meat. cheese pie is sirnica
Livno highland food postcard beyond the café street

grammar.title: Volim + object
grammar.explanation: Volim means I love or I like. Put the food after it as a ready chunk: Volim burek. Volim kahvu. For many feminine food nouns ending in -a, the spoken object often ends in -u: Volim sirnicu. Volim zeljanicu. Learn the pairs as phrases first. Do not memorize a full case table today.

grammar.title: Ne volim
grammar.explanation: Add ne before volim to say you do not like something: Ne volim luk. Ne volim čaj. Keep it soft and clear. You can still be polite while you refuse a filling.

grammar.title: Gladan / gladna
grammar.explanation: Match the adjective to who is speaking. Emir says Ja sam gladan. Ana says Ja sam gladna. Then order food and finish with Dobar tek!

culture.title: Burek is meat, and Livno sends cheese
culture.body: On a Bosnian street, burek means a meat pita. Ask for cheese and you want sirnica. Spinach or greens mean zeljanica. Emir takes Ana to a buregdžinica near Amira’s, then shows a postcard from Livno in western Bosnia: highland pastures famous for Livanjski sir. The café is HQ, but the country’s food map is wider than one warm tray. Today Ana learns to say what she loves before the first bite turns into a flaky disaster.

lessonBlocks.title: Lesson A: Food words on the tray
lessonBlocks.body: Name the classics: burek (meat), sirnica (cheese), zeljanica (greens), pita as the general phyllo pie word. Add hljeb, jogurt, meso, sir, voće, povrće. Say each twice. Mark the BiH spelling hljeb. Emir points at the tray and refuses the tourist trap sentence burek sa sirom. In Bosnian that fight is real: burek is with meat.
tips: burek = meat; sirnica = cheese; zeljanica = greens
Type hljeb with lj, not a soft English h-leb guess

lessonBlocks.title: Lesson B: Volim / ne volim at the counter
lessonBlocks.body: Build today’s kit: Volim burek. Volim sirnicu. Ne volim luk. Ja sam gladna / gladan. Ukusno! Dobar tek! Ana tries a too-hot bite, drops flakes on Mrvica, and still finishes the sentence. Food disasters are allowed. Silent pointing is not the goal.
tips: Chunk: Volim… / Ne volim… / Dobar tek!
Use gladna if you are Ana; gladan if you are Emir

conversation.title: Burek katastrofa

funFacts.title: No cheese in the word burek
funFacts.body: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, asking for burek sa sirom is a classic tourist tell. Locals hear burek as meat. Cheese pie is sirnica.

funFacts.title: Livanjski sir
funFacts.body: Livno’s highland cheese tradition sits west of Sarajevo’s street trays. Emir’s postcard is a reminder that dairy fame is not only a city story.

funFacts.title: Jogurt is a partner
funFacts.body: Warm burek often arrives with jogurt. The pair cools the bite and turns a snack into a small ritual.

funFacts.title: Mrvica tax
funFacts.body: Any flaky pita near Mrvica becomes a shared meal whether you planned it or not.

civicContext.title: Local food culture, imported staples
civicContext.body: Bosnia and Herzegovina still depends heavily on imported food even though street food and home cooking are central to daily life. After the war, fragmented farmland and weak agricultural investment slowed the recovery of domestic production, so bakeries and shops often stock flour, oil, dairy, and other staples from abroad. Local pita culture is strong, but the grocery supply behind it is still shaped by that import dependence.
